indicators: Domain: micr0soft-support.com (typosquatting using zero instead of letter 'o')
Email sender IP: 198.51.100.45 (hosted on bulletproof VPS known for phishing)
Email fails DMARC alignment (header.from domain microsoft.com vs sender domain micr0soft-support.com)
Phishing URL uses HTTP and redirects to legitimate-looking URL parameter
Web server logs show POST requests with credential parameters
WAF detects credential fields in POST request and raises alerts
MFA triggered and blocked unauthorized login attempts despite stolen credentials
example.detection_method: Combine advanced email filtering with SPF/DKIM/DMARC checks and suspicious domain lookups; monitor web server logs and WAF alerts for POST requests containing typical credential fields; correlate login attempts with MFA logs to detect failed or suspicious second-factor attempts; conduct user education to recognize typosquatting domains and obfuscated URLs; use sandboxing to analyze email content and links.
relevant_mitre_techniques: T1531 - Account Access Removal (attempted via credential theft)
T1110 - Brute Force (if attacker uses stolen credentials later)

validation.comments: The sample accurately represents a social engineering credential harvesting attack via spear-phishing email. The scenario description clearly aligns with the problem nature, describing impersonation of a trusted entity (Microsoft Office 365) and use of a lookalike domain with obfuscated URL to trick users into submitting credentials. The technical data is comprehensive and realistic, including detailed email headers showing SPF/DKIM passes but DMARC failure, a plausible spear-phishing email body with a suspicious HTTP link using a typosquatted domain, SMTP transaction logs, domain registration info indicating recent creation and privacy protection, phishing URL obfuscation analysis, web server logs showing credential submission, WAF alerts detecting credential fields, and MFA logs showing detection of unauthorized login attempts. The indicators section clearly explains why this sample matches the problem, highlighting domain typosquatting, email sender IP reputation, DMARC failure, URL obfuscation, web logs, WAF alerts, and MFA intervention. The detection method is thorough and appropriate, covering email filtering, domain checks, log monitoring, MFA correlation, user training, and sandboxing. Relevant MITRE techniques are well chosen and relevant to the attack stages. Overall, the sample is complete, realistic, and correctly aligned with the stated cybersecurity problem and risk reduction strategies.
